questiontext.text: Which of the following is a valid Java variable name?

generalfeedback.text: Variable names are case-sensitive, cannot start with a digit or contain spaces, and cannot be reserved words.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: Identifiers cannot begin with a digit.
Correct: starts with a letter; letters/digits/_/$ are allowed; no spaces.
This is a reserved word (keyword) and cannot be used as an identifier.
Hyphens are not allowed in identifiers; use camelCase like totalSum.

questiontext.text: Which statement about Java variable names is true?

generalfeedback.text: Identifiers are case-sensitive; permitted characters are letters, digits, _, and $, but they cannot start with a digit.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: Incorrect: total and Total are different identifiers.
Incorrect: spaces are not permitted in identifiers.
Correct: Java treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different.

answer.text: They can begin with a digit

feedback.text: Incorrect: identifiers cannot begin with a digit.

questiontext.text: In Java, a ________ is a small, meaningful piece of code such as a keyword, operator, literal, or identifier.

generalfeedback.text: Tokens include keywords, identifiers, literals, operators, and separators.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: A block is a group of statements enclosed in braces.
Correct: tokens are the smallest meaningful units recognized by the compiler.
A method is a named block of code that can be invoked.
Comments are not tokens and are ignored by the compiler.

questiontext.text: Which declaration correctly defines a float variable with the value 4.5?

generalfeedback.text: Use float with an f suffix (e.g., 3.14f) or use double without the suffix.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: A float literal must use the f (or F) suffix.
Correct: the f suffix makes the literal type float.
This declares a double, not a float.
Non-integer literal cannot be assigned to an int.

questiontext.text: Which operator would you use to calculate the remainder of an integer division in Java?

generalfeedback.text: Use % to compute the remainder: e.g., 10 % 6 is 4.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: This performs division, not the remainder.
This performs multiplication.
Correct: the modulo operator % returns the remainder.
Double slash is not an operator in Java; it starts a comment.

questiontext.text: What is wrong with the declaration Int number = 5;

generalfeedback.text: Primitive types are lowercase (e.g., int, double, boolean).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: The variable name number is fine.

answer.text: Value cannot be assigned at declaration

feedback.text: Assignment at declaration is allowed.
Correct: the primitive type is int, not Int.
There is a semicolon present.

questiontext.text: What is the result of 10 / 6 in Java when both operands are integers?

generalfeedback.text: If both operands are int, the result is int with the fractional part discarded.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: Correct: integer division truncates toward zero; the fractional part is discarded.
This would require floating-point division.
Floating-point approximation; not for integer division.
This is the mathematical quotient, but Java integer division truncates to 1.

questiontext.text: Which statement about local variables is true?

generalfeedback.text: Local variables are short-lived and scoped to the block in which they are declared.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

answer.text: They exist for the lifetime of the program

feedback.text: No: they do not outlive the method/block.

answer.text: They exist only while the method is executing

feedback.text: Correct: locals are created on entry and discarded on exit.

answer.text: They can be accessed from anywhere in the class

feedback.text: No: their scope is limited to their declaring block.

answer.text: They must always receive their value from parameters

feedback.text: No: locals are set inside the method; parameters receive values from callers.

generalfeedback.text: The method copies balance into a local, clears the field, and returns the saved value.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: No: the method stores the old balance in amountToRefund before clearing.
Correct: amountToRefund holds the prior balance.
After setting balance = 0, the new value is 0, but the method returns amountToRefund.
This method returns an int and has a return statement.

questiontext.text: What happens when a return statement is executed in a method?

generalfeedback.text: A return immediately ends method execution and hands back control (and optionally a value) to the caller.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

answer.text: The method continues executing until the end

feedback.text: No: execution stops at the return.
Correct: control returns to the caller immediately.

answer.text: The method skips one line and continues

feedback.text: No: return exits the method.

answer.text: The method pauses but does not terminate

feedback.text: No: there is no pause; it exits.

questiontext.text: The scope of a field is:

generalfeedback.text: A field belongs to the class and is visible throughout it (visibility may be further restricted by access modifiers).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

answer.text: The block in which it is declared

feedback.text: This describes a local variable, not a field.
Correct: a field is accessible throughout its class (subject to access modifiers).
Fields are not declared inside methods; locals are.
This is not how field scope works.

name.text: Q12 – Lifetime of a local variable

questiontext.text: The lifetime of a local variable is:

generalfeedback.text: Local variables are created when their block begins execution and are discarded when it ends.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Review the slides on this topic.

feedback.text: Locals do not persist for the whole program.

answer.text: The lifetime of its containing object

feedback.text: That describes fields, not locals.

answer.text: The execution of the block in which it is declared

feedback.text: Correct: locals exist only during execution of their block.

answer.text: Until the class is garbage collected

feedback.text: GC pertains to objects on the heap, not stack-allocated locals.
